topic: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Transverse and longitudinal waves
subject: physics

items.q: Which statement about the types of wave is correct?
items.correct: A wave is either transverse or longitudinal.
items.misconception: All waves are transverse, as diagrams show.
items.why: The first waves met in science are drawn as curves, and the everyday image of a wave is a hump of water, so the transverse picture becomes the definition of a wave. Sound in air is longitudinal: it has no wavy shape in space at all, only compressions and rarefactions. Every wave in this topic is one type or the other.
items.random_wrong: The type depends on how the wave is drawn.

items.q: Ripples on a water surface are an example of which type of wave, and for what reason?
items.correct: Transverse: the surface moves up and down as the ripple moves outwards.
items.misconception: Longitudinal: the water is pushed outwards from where the stone landed.
items.why: The ripples clearly spread outwards from the source, and 'pushed outwards' sounds like the pushing that makes a compression in a longitudinal wave. Spreading outwards is the direction the wave travels, not the direction of the oscillation. The oscillation is up and down, at right angles to that, so the ripples are transverse.
items.random_wrong: Longitudinal: each bit of water travels along with the ripple it is in.

items.q: A small polystyrene ball floats in a ripple tank while straight ripples pass beneath it. What does the ball do?
items.correct: It bobs up and down in the same place as each ripple passes.
items.misconception: It is carried along with the ripples to the far end of the tank.
items.why: Ripples look like moving humps of water, and the word 'wave' is used in everyday speech for water that is actually moving, as in a wave breaking on a beach. A floating ball shows what the water does: it bobs up and down in the same place as ripple after ripple passes under it, and is not carried to the far bank. Only the ripple crosses the pond.
items.random_wrong: It moves back and forth along the direction the ripples travel.

items.q: In a sound wave travelling through air, what is a compression?
items.correct: A region where the air particles are pushed closer together.
items.misconception: A region where the air particles are squashed into a smaller size.
items.why: The word 'compression' is used in everyday life for squashing an object, such as a sponge, so it is applied to the particles rather than to the spaces between them. Particles cannot be squashed. What changes is their spacing: in a compression they are closer together, in a rarefaction further apart, and the particles themselves are unchanged.
items.random_wrong: A region where the air particles are held still by the pressure.

items.q: What is a rarefaction in a sound wave travelling through air?
items.correct: A region where the air particles are further apart than normal.
items.misconception: A region of totally empty space with no air particles inside it.
items.why: 'Rarefaction' is an unfamiliar word, and diagrams drawn as rows of dots leave visible gaps that look like empty regions. A rarefaction still contains particles; the density and pressure there are simply lower than normal. Nothing about a sound wave in air removes the air from a region.
items.random_wrong: A region where the air particles have stopped vibrating for now.

items.q: A loudspeaker cone moves forwards and backwards. What does this produce in the air in front of it?
items.correct: Compressions and rarefactions travelling outwards through the air.
items.misconception: A stream of air pushed out from the cone towards the listener.
items.why: Sound comes from something moving, and it is easy to picture the movement as air being pushed all the way from the source to the listener. If air travelled from the source to the listener there would be a wind from every sound source and the air by it would run out. Neither happens: the air vibrates in place and passes the wave on.
items.random_wrong: Side-to-side ripples in the air, like ripples on a water surface.

items.q: How do the density and pressure of the air compare in a compression and in a rarefaction?
items.correct: Both are higher in a compression and lower in a rarefaction.
items.misconception: Air pressure is higher in a compression; a rarefaction has none.
items.why: 'Rarefaction' is an unfamiliar word, and diagrams drawn as rows of dots leave visible gaps that look like empty regions. A rarefaction still contains particles; the density and pressure there are simply lower than normal. Nothing about a sound wave in air removes the air from a region.
items.random_wrong: Both stay the same, since only the spacing of particles changes.

items.q: In a transverse wave, how do the oscillations compare with the direction the wave travels?
items.correct: They are at right angles to the direction the wave travels.
items.misconception: They are always up and down, whichever way the wave goes.
items.why: Nearly every textbook picture shows a transverse wave drawn across the page with the oscillations vertical, so 'up and down' gets learned instead of 'at right angles'. A rope hanging down and shaken sideways carries a transverse wave: the oscillation is horizontal and the wave goes up. What matters is the angle between the two directions, not which way is up.
items.random_wrong: They are along the direction the wave travels, as in sound.

items.q: A rope hangs down from a hook. A student shakes the bottom end from side to side and a wave travels up the rope. Which type of wave is it?
items.correct: Transverse, because the oscillation is at right angles to the travel.
items.misconception: Longitudinal, because the movement is sideways here, not up and down.
items.why: Nearly every textbook picture shows a transverse wave drawn across the page with the oscillations vertical, so 'up and down' gets learned instead of 'at right angles'. A rope hanging down and shaken sideways carries a transverse wave: the oscillation is horizontal and the wave goes up. What matters is the angle between the two directions, not which way is up.
items.random_wrong: Longitudinal, because the wave travels along the length of the rope.

items.q: A slinky lying on a bench is pushed and pulled along its own length. Which description of the wave that travels along it is correct?
items.correct: Coils vibrate along the slinky, making compressions and rarefactions.
items.misconception: Coils travel from one end of the slinky to the other with the wave.
items.why: The compressions really do travel the length of the slinky, and it is hard to see that the material forming them changes as they go. Watch one marked coil: it moves back and forth a short distance and returns, while compressions carry on past it to the far end. The wave travels; the coils do not.
items.random_wrong: Coils vibrate up and down, so this must be a transverse wave instead.

items.q: Which of these is evidence that it is the sound wave, and not the air, that crosses a room?
items.correct: You can hear a distant loudspeaker with no draught reaching you.
items.misconception: A loudspeaker blows dust off its cone when the volume is high.
items.why: Sound comes from something moving, and it is easy to picture the movement as air being pushed all the way from the source to the listener. If air travelled from the source to the listener there would be a wind from every sound source and the air by it would run out. Neither happens: the air vibrates in place and passes the wave on.
items.random_wrong: Each air particle travels from the loudspeaker to the listener.

items.q: Ripples cross a pond and reach the far bank. What does this tell you about the water in the pond?
items.correct: Each part of the surface moves up and down as the ripple goes by.
items.misconception: The water at the near bank has moved across to the far bank now.
items.why: Ripples look like moving humps of water, and the word 'wave' is used in everyday speech for water that is actually moving, as in a wave breaking on a beach. A floating ball shows what the water does: it bobs up and down in the same place as ripple after ripple passes under it, and is not carried to the far bank. Only the ripple crosses the pond.
items.random_wrong: The water moves across the pond at the same speed as the ripple.

items.q: Suppose the air really did travel along with a sound wave. What would a listener notice?
items.correct: A wind blowing out from the source whenever a sound was made.
items.misconception: Nothing new at all, because sound already is a movement of air.
items.why: Sound comes from something moving, and it is easy to picture the movement as air being pushed all the way from the source to the listener. If air travelled from the source to the listener there would be a wind from every sound source and the air by it would run out. Neither happens: the air vibrates in place and passes the wave on.
items.random_wrong: Each particle vibrating about a fixed point, just as it does now.

items.q: Sound travelling through air is compared with ripples on a water surface. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Sound oscillates along its direction of travel; ripples oscillate across it.
items.misconception: Both are transverse waves, because both can be drawn as a wavy curve.
items.why: The trace on an oscilloscope and the wavy line in a diagram are graphs of how pressure changes; students read them as a picture of the wave's shape in space. The wavy line is a graph, not a photograph of the air. In the air itself the particles vibrate along the direction the sound travels, which makes sound longitudinal.
items.random_wrong: Both are longitudinal waves, because both spread outwards from a source.

items.q: Are the particles in a compression moving?
items.correct: Yes. They are vibrating back and forth about their own fixed positions.
items.misconception: In a compression the particles are packed tight and held still while the wave moves on.
items.why: Static diagrams show compressions as fixed clusters of dots, so the particles look frozen in place rather than vibrating. The particles keep vibrating all the time. A compression forms where the vibrations happen to bring particles close together, and the region of crowding moves on as they carry on vibrating.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How fast do the particles move compared with the wave?
items.correct: The wave travels much faster and much further than any individual particle moves.
items.misconception: The particles travel along at the same speed and in the same direction as the wave.
items.why: The wave is described as 'moving through the material', which sounds as though the material is moving with it at the same rate. A ripple crosses a whole pond while a floating ball moves only a few centimetres up and down. The disturbance is passed from particle to particle, so it can travel far further than any particle does.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is happening in the gaps between compressions?
items.correct: Those regions are rarefactions, where the particles are further apart than normal.
items.misconception: The gaps between compressions are just empty spaces where nothing is going on.
items.why: Compressions are the striking feature of diagrams, so the regions between them are read as background rather than as a part of the wave. A longitudinal wave shows areas of compression and rarefaction. The rarefactions are as much a part of the wave as the compressions and carry the lower pressure of it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What decides whether a wave is transverse or longitudinal?
items.correct: The direction of the oscillations compared with the direction of travel decides it.
items.misconception: It depends on how the wave is drawn: curvy lines are transverse, rows of dots are longitudinal.
items.why: The two types are usually introduced through their standard diagrams, so the diagram style is remembered as the definition instead of as a way of representing it. The same longitudinal wave can be drawn as rows of dots or as a graph shaped like a curve. What classifies it is the physical behaviour of the material, not the choice of diagram.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which direction do you look at to classify a wave?
items.correct: Both: the oscillation direction is compared with the direction of travel.
items.misconception: It is the direction the wave travels in that decides which type of wave it is.
items.why: 'Longitudinal' sounds like 'along', so students match it to a wave that travels along something such as a rope or a slinky. A rope can carry either type. Shake the end sideways and the wave is transverse; push and pull the end along the rope and it is longitudinal. Only the oscillation direction differs.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
